findings: Plan names no edit set or module locations for the checks it owns: The plan says this child owns P1/P5/P6/P7 (and now P8), the wiring of P2/P3/P4 into the DET floor, the 'exec=DET' code-executor dispatch path and coverage on the attestation. It does not name one file, module, function or schema to create or change. The repository the tools can read has only README.md ('eval fixture') and .rebar/hlc.state, so none of the targets (the orchestrator, the code executor, the attestation model, the size-handling ladder) can be found from the plan. Only the consumed facade, rebar.grounding.{refute_absence,applies,scan}, resolves, and only in the installed environment. An implementer can't tell where the checks go or which existing contracts they must fit.

Title, What and first AC still say P1–P7 after P8 was added: P8 was appended as an 'added' section, but the title ('P1-P7'), the What list and the first AC ('P1-P7 implemented ... fail-open tested per tool') were not updated. The later AC says 'P1–P8 run as the deterministic exec=DET tier'. The checklist therefore disagrees on scope: P8 has no implementation/fail-open/test AC that matches the others, and it is unclear whether P8 is part of the 'polyglot, fail-open' contract.

Fail-open as 'ironclad' PASS lets the only blocking tier pass vacuously: The DET floor is described as the only blocking tier, yet every abstain (no tool installed, unsupported language, parse error, timeout) counts as PASS. In an environment without ctags/scc/syft or network access, P2/P3/P4 all abstain and the floor blocks nothing, and nothing gates on that. The only mitigation is 'Coverage recorded on the attestation', which has no consumer, no minimum-coverage rule and no requirement to show a skipped check differently from a real pass. The approach may be intended, but the plan never weighs this failure mode or says how a fully skipped floor is shown to the user.

P3 deps.dev registry lookup conflicts with the 'frozen, deterministic' floor: P3 checks package existence against the deps.dev registry, a live network service. Its results change over time (packages get published or yanked) and with network state, so the same plan can PASS or FAIL on different days or machines. That contradicts the stated goal of a 'frozen, deterministic' floor. It also sends dependency names from tickets to an outside service. The plan does not mention pinning, caching, an offline mode or a timeout budget.

Rebar-owned checks P1, P5, P6, P7 are named but not specified: These are the checks this child actually builds, and each gets only a label: 'readiness-shape', 'task-DAG validity + interference', 'AC/DD quality', 'destructive/irreversible sniff (escalates T4)'. The plan does not say what input each check reads, what rule decides FAIL, what 'interference' means, how 'AC/DD quality' can be judged deterministically without an LLM, or what 'escalates T4' does mechanically when the DET tier is the blocking one. They cannot be built or tested without clarification.

P8 threshold and token estimator are undefined: P8 fails when content 'exceeds — or is anticipated to exceed — the largest configured context window'. The plan does not say where the context-window config lives, which tokenizer or estimator is used, what 'anticipated' means (a safety margin?), or how prompt overhead for one criterion per call is counted. Without these the check is neither reproducible nor testable. Its relation to P4 oversize thresholds is also left open.

Two different emission paths for P8: One section says P8 is emitted by the orchestrator 'during the size-handling ladder'. The later AC says P1–P8 all run as the exec=DET tier dispatched through the code executor. These are different paths, and it is not stated whether P8 runs once, twice, or which path is authoritative.

Blocking-posture statements contradict each other: The Why says the DET floor is 'the ONLY blocking tier' and that every LLM criterion is advisory. The third AC says DET is only the default blocking tier and that LLM criteria can opt into blocking through block_threshold, 'not an architectural limit'. The plan needs one consistent posture so tests and docs know what to assert.

Testing plan covers only fail-open, not check correctness: The only test AC is 'fail-open (skipped=pass) tested per tool'. There are no tests that each check fires on a positive case: a real missing symbol for P2, a nonexistent package for P3, a cyclic DAG for P5, a destructive operation for P7, an oversized ticket for P8. Nothing tests the coverage/attestation recording or the exec=DET dispatch either. A floor that always abstains would pass these ACs.

The rebar-owned checks P1 (readiness-shape), P5 (DAG validity + interference), P6 (AC/DD quality) and P7 (destructive sniff) are only named. Their deterministic rules are not specified: what shape counts as 'ready', what 'interference' means between tasks, which AC/DD properties are checked without an LLM, and which patterns P7 sniffs. An executor must invent the semantics of the only blocking tier.

P7 says it 'escalates T4', but the escalation mechanism is undefined. Is it a FAIL, an advisory finding, a flag that forces the T4 LLM overlay to run, or something that raises block_threshold? 'T4' is also undefined in this plan.

P7 (destructive/irreversible sniff) is described only as 'escalates T4'. The plan doesn't say whether a P7 hit fails the blocking DET floor or only routes to T4. A heuristic sniff that can block works against the fail-open stance of the floor: a false positive would block a plan outright, with no abstain path.

P8 depends on two inputs from the LLM configuration: 'the largest configured context window' and a token estimate. The plan does not say what P8 does when no context window is configured, when the window cannot be read, or when the token estimate cannot be computed (unknown model or tokenizer). It is also not tied to the floor's 'abstain -> skipped = PASS' contract. The token-estimate method is not named either, so the 'anticipated to exceed' decision rule is not specified next to the check that needs it.

P8's size test is under-specified. The plan does not define the token-estimation method (tokenizer or chars/4 heuristic), what 'anticipated to exceed' means operationally, where 'the largest configured context window' is read from, how the prompt/rubric overhead of 'one-criterion-per-call' is counted, or which 'container criteria' trigger the parent+child pairing.

The title and AC promise to build and per-tool-test 'polyglot tool wrappers', but the scope says this child does NOT re-build the tooling and only consumes the 8f6c facade. Implementers may re-wrap ctags/syft/scc/lizard or write per-tool tests that belong to 8f6c.

The title ('fail-open polyglot tool wrappers') and AC1 ('fail-open (skipped=pass) tested per tool') read as if this child writes and tests its own wrappers around ctags/deps.dev/syft/scc/lizard. That contradicts Scope, which says this child consumes the shipped 8f6c facade 'as a library, not as new integrations' and 'does NOT re-build it'. Implementers could rebuild per-tool wrappers or tool-level abstain logic that already exists in the oracle.

P8 FAILs (blocking, DET) when content is 'anticipated (token-estimate) to exceed the largest configured context window', but the plan never names the estimator. Token counts depend on the model, and the vendor's own counting API makes a network call and documents its result as an estimate. A purely deterministic, offline check therefore has to use a local tokenizer or a heuristic (e.g., about 4 chars per token), and none of these options or their error margins are discussed. That matters for a check that blocks.

The ACs only verify the fail-open (skipped=PASS) path and the tier wiring. No AC requires that each check actually DETECTS its defect on a positive fixture. Examples: P2 flags a nonexistent symbol, P3 flags a nonexistent package, P5 flags a cycle, P8 flags an oversize ticket. The union of ACs therefore does not prove that the floor catches anything.

Every AC is satisfiable by a floor that never blocks anything. Testing is only specified for the fail-open (skipped=pass) path. No AC requires a fixture showing each check FAILS on a true defect, e.g.: a missing file/symbol for P2, a nonexistent package for P3, a cyclic task DAG for P5, a destructive command for P7, an over-window ticket for P8.

The plan doesn't say how P2 (file/symbol/import resolution) can ever FAIL. It sends P2 through the oracle's `refute_absence` facade, whose contract is described only as 'abstain-by-default' with abstain = PASS. A facade that refutes absence proves something exists. Its non-pass outcomes may only be 'refuted (exists)' or 'abstain', which leaves no outcome that confirms a referenced file or symbol is missing. If so, P2 can never flag a hallucinated reference, and it becomes a check that can't block.

P3 uses the deps.dev registry for package existence inside what the plan calls a 'frozen, deterministic polyglot floor', but that claim is not checked against what deps.dev actually is. deps.dev is a live, continuously updated network service. It indexes only a fixed set of public ecosystems (Go, RubyGems, npm, Cargo, Maven, PyPI, NuGet, plus Gradle plugins). It does not cover private or internal registries or ecosystems such as Packagist, Hex, CocoaPods, pub or CRAN. A deps.dev 'not found' therefore does not prove a package is missing, and the same input can give different results over time. The plan never says how a deps.dev miss maps to a result: abstain (pass) or a blocking FAIL.

P2 promises 'file/symbol/import resolution' through universal-ctags, but ctags does not resolve imports. By default it tags definitions. Import statements show up only as syntactic reference tags (role 'imported'), only when the reference extra is enabled (--extras=+r, off by default), and only in the parsers that implement it. The plan does not say which languages actually get import checking, or that a missing reference tag must count as abstain rather than 'import absent'.

No acceptance criterion has a proving command. 'Coverage recorded on the attestation' does not say what coverage is: per-check ran/abstained/failed, per-language, per-tool? It also gives no field name or schema, so it cannot be verified.
AC1 bundles seven distinct checks with effort framing ('implemented in Python'). It is near epic-scale for a single criterion and hard to complete or verify in one session as a single unit.

The unit bundles eight checks plus a new orchestrator execution path. Most checks are independently valuable, testable and releasable (P1 readiness-shape, P5 DAG/interference, P6 AC/DD quality, P7 destructive sniff, P8 reviewability). There is no sequencing or thin-slice MVP that de-risks the riskiest piece (the exec=DET dispatch path plus facade wiring) first.

The Why section requires a 'frozen, deterministic' floor, but P3 queries the live deps.dev registry. Registry availability and contents change over time, so the same ticket can PASS (abstain on timeout) on one run and FAIL on another. The plan does not state how determinism is preserved (pinned snapshot, cache, recorded response) or the network/timeout/rate-limit constraints.

P3 checks package existence against the live deps.dev registry. That contradicts the stated goal of a 'frozen, deterministic' floor. Registry contents change (packages get published or yanked, and slopsquatted names appear), and network availability varies. The same plan can pass or fail on different runs, inside the only tier that blocks.

The T8 AC says P1-P8 are dispatched by the orchestrator's code executor as the exec=DET tier. The P8 section instead says 'the orchestrator emits it during the size-handling ladder'. It is unclear whether P8 is a DET-tier check run by the code executor or an orchestrator-internal emission, which affects where it is implemented.

No edit-set, and the code it builds on is not in the repo: The plan does not name a single file, module, service or workflow to create or change. The repository has nothing for it to plug into: no queue for `Autosubmit` changes, no Gerrit integration, no CI workflow and no Phase 1 code. The plan says it 'Depends on Phase 1' but does not link that work, and no ticket can be found for it. As written, an implementer has to invent the architecture: where the batcher runs, how it reads the queue, and how it talks to Gerrit and GHA.

Atomic submit depends on Verified-casting, which is out of scope: Scope moves Verified-casting to a separate story. But the submit criterion ('On green, submits the whole batch atomically') needs something to turn a green CI run into a submittable state in Gerrit. Usually that is a Verified+1 label on every change in the chain, not just the tip. Without Verified-casting, either Gerrit refuses the submit or this story has to cast votes on its own, which duplicates the other story. As scoped, the acceptance criteria cannot be met independently.

'Tested tip == landed tree' is not protected against `main` moving: The batch is assembled on the current `main` tip, then waits a full CI cycle. If `main` moves in that time (a human submit or another batch), Gerrit's submit types such as Rebase If Necessary or Merge If Necessary will produce a tree that was never tested. Fast Forward Only will reject the submit instead. The plan picks no submit strategy and has no compare-and-abort step to keep its own acceptance criterion true.

Batch-size bound mixes up runs, jobs and changes, and rests on an unchecked premise: The batch-size criterion bounds 'batch size' to 'one CI run's job budget', justified by a cap of about 3 concurrent runs. That cap limits concurrent runs, not jobs inside one run. If CI runs once on the combined tip, the job count does not depend on how many changes are in the batch, so this bound limits nothing. The '~3 concurrent runs' Free-tier figure is stated without a source, and GHA's documented free-plan limit is on concurrent jobs, not runs. The bound cannot be measured as written, and the plan does not say where it will be documented.

No mechanism for triggering GHA from a Gerrit chain: GitHub Actions does not trigger natively on Gerrit changes. To 'trigger exactly ONE CI run on the combined tip', something has to push the combined tip to a ref GHA watches, or call workflow_dispatch/repository_dispatch, and then get the result back to Gerrit. The plan says nothing about this, and the repo has no workflow to extend. Without it, the criterion of exactly one CI run per batch cannot be implemented or checked.

Assembly is unspecified: rebase conflicts, new patchsets and approvals: To put independent stacks into one linear chain, the stacks have to be re-parented onto each other, which creates new patchsets. The plan does not say what happens when a stack does not rebase cleanly (drop it, end the batch, or order stacks differently). It also does not say how stacks are ordered, or whether rebasing keeps the existing Code-Review approvals, which depends on the label's copy conditions. If approvals are lost, the combined chain cannot be submitted.

No testing plan: The plan has no tests or verification approach for any acceptance criterion. Nothing checks that a single run happens per batch, that an N-change batch lands atomically, that the landed SHA equals the tested SHA, or that the size bound is enforced. The criteria are stated as outcomes, with no evidence kind such as unit tests against a fake Gerrit or an end-to-end run.

The wall-clock benefit depends on out-of-scope failure handling, and there is no rollback: The value claim (collapsing ~N×CI to ~1 CI cycle) only holds when the batch is green. With batch-failure handling scoped out, a single bad change makes the whole batch fail, with no bisection or eviction. Every queued change is then blocked, possibly worse than landing serially. The plan also has no feature flag or fallback to serial landing while failure handling is missing.

The claim that the landed tree equals the tested tip, and that ancestor submit is atomic, rests on an unverified Gerrit project configuration. If the submit type is REBASE_IF_NECESSARY, REBASE_ALWAYS or CHERRY_PICK, or main moves between the CI start and the submit, Gerrit lands rewritten commits whose tree was never tested.

The plan says 'the tested tip == the landed tree' but has no mechanism to enforce it. Between the CI trigger and the submit, main can advance or someone can upload a new patchset to a change in the chain. With a rebasing or cherry-pick submit type, Gerrit would then land a tree CI never tested. This is a check-then-act (TOCTOU) race.

The plan asserts Gerrit can do an 'ancestor-atomic submit' where 'the tested tip == the landed tree' without saying which Gerrit submit type or settings make that true. Under the default Merge If Necessary, or under Rebase if Necessary, Gerrit creates a merge commit or rebases at submit time if main has moved since CI. The landed tree then differs from the tested tip. Gerrit's own maintainers describe ancestor submission as only 'pseudo atomic'.

'Ancestor-atomic submit' is asserted, but the plan never names the Gerrit submit surface (REST POST /changes/{id}/submit, or submitWholeTopic) or the project submit type. 'The tested tip == the landed tree' only holds if the submit type creates no new commits. With REBASE_IF_NECESSARY, REBASE_ALWAYS, MERGE_IF_NECESSARY or MERGE_ALWAYS, Gerrit rebases or merges when `main` has moved during the CI run. In that case the landed tree is not the tree CI tested.

The 'tested tip == landed tree' guarantee has no mechanism for the case where main advances between CI start and submit. The plan also does not specify the Gerrit submit type, e.g. fast-forward-only, or abort-if-main-moved.

The plan does not handle main advancing, or a batched change receiving a new patchset or losing its Autosubmit vote, between the CI trigger and the submit. In those cases AC3's guarantee 'the tested tip == the landed tree' cannot hold, and the plan does not say whether to abort, re-batch or rebase.

The assembly algorithm leaves several decisions undecided. It does not say how independent stacks are ordered in the combined chain, what happens on a rebase/cherry-pick conflict between stacks during assembly, or what triggers a batch (time window, queue threshold, or on every Autosubmit vote).

Atomic land on green is in scope, but verified-casting is declared a separate story. The plan does not say how a green run makes the chain submittable, e.g. whether Gerrit requires Verified+1 that this story cannot cast.
The plan never says what happens when assembling the combined linear chain fails because a queued change or stack does not rebase cleanly onto main or onto the preceding stack.

The plan does not define when batch assembly fires: immediately on the first Autosubmit vote, on a timer or collection window, or when the previous batch finishes. This trigger determines both the latency of a single change and whether batching yields any wall-clock gain.

AC3 requires the batch to be submitted, but Gerrit submit normally requires a Verified label on each change, and the plan defers 'Verified-casting' to a separate story. The plan does not state how AC3 is satisfiable, or provable, within this story.

The plan doesn't say how independent stacks become one linear chain. Doing it means re-parenting changes, which uploads new patchsets. The plan doesn't cover rebase conflicts between stacks, whether Code-Review approvals carry over to the new patchsets, or who is recorded as uploader. Conflicts during assembly are part of assembly, not the 'batch-failure handling' that was scoped out.

Submitting with ancestors in Gerrit needs every change in the chain to be submittable, which includes the Verified label. The Scope section moves 'Verified-casting' to a separate story, so this story's atomic land (AC3) depends on functionality it doesn't deliver. One green combined-tip run also has to turn into Verified on every ancestor change, but the plan doesn't link the two.

Gerrit only submits a tip together with its ancestors if every ancestor is submittable on its own (Verified, Code-Review and the other labels). The plan triggers CI once on the tip and puts Verified-casting in another story. It never says how ancestors get a passing Verified vote, so ancestor submit may be rejected.

The batch-size bound is deferred to the executor instead of decided. AC4 says the bound 'fits the GHA concurrency cap' and 'documents the bound', but never states the number or how it is derived. It also conflates the per-run job budget with the ~3 concurrent-runs cap from Why.

The unit of the batch bound in AC4 is ambiguous. 'one CI run's job budget' is a per-run job count, while the stated constraint is a cap of about 3 concurrent runs. The plan does not say whether the bound counts changes, stacks, or GHA jobs, or how a change's job cost is estimated.

AC4 bounds batch size by 'one CI run's job budget (fits the GHA concurrency cap)'. But the whole design runs a single workflow on the combined tip, so a bigger batch doesn't use more concurrent runs. The concurrency cap doesn't govern batch size. What actually grows with batch size is the chance a batch fails and how much work it takes to find which change broke it, plus how long a run on the combined tree takes or whether it hits a timeout. The bound is tied to a stand-in for the real constraint.

No AC has a proving command or check. Nothing shows how 'exactly ONE CI run' is counted, how tree equality is asserted, or how linearity is checked. There is also no end-to-end exercise against live Gerrit + GHA, even though the whole path crosses those external boundaries.

Assembly reparents independent authors' stacks onto each other by uploading new patch sets. The plan neither acknowledges this user-visible rewrite nor provides a back-out that restores the original parents if the batch is not landed.

The 'exactly ONE CI run' criterion contradicts the bounded re-batch loop: One acceptance criterion requires exactly one CI run on the combined tip. The TOCTOU criterion requires re-assembling and re-batching each time main advances, up to N=5 times. Each re-assembly produces a new combined-tip SHA, so it needs a new CI run (otherwise the handed-off tested_sha would not match the tree). A batch can therefore trigger up to 6 runs, and both criteria cannot be satisfied as written. The plan also does not say whether a re-batch cancels or reuses the earlier run, or which run_id goes into the handoff record.

The TOCTOU re-check happens at handoff, but the submit happens later in S8: The re-check runs 'immediately before the batch is handed off for submit'. After the handoff, S8 still casts a Verified vote on every member and then submits. main can move during that window, so the check does not protect the moment that matters (submit). The plan says it will 'never hand off a stale tree', but staleness at submit time is not covered by S7 or by any contract S7 places on S8.

The handoff record cannot bind each member's vote to the SHA that was assembled: The plan says S8 'binds each vote to a SHA S7 actually assembled + tested'. But the record holds only change IDs plus one tested_sha (the combined tip). Assembly rebases every member and creates new patchsets for them. S8 casts Verified per member on a specific revision, so it needs each member's assembled patchset number or commit SHA. Without them, S8 cannot check that the revision it votes on is the one inside the tested chain.

No behaviour is defined for conflicts during cross-stack assembly: The Why section and the algorithm both assume the N changes are 'non-conflicting'. Neither the What section nor the acceptance criteria say how conflicts are detected, or what happens when stacking stack B onto stack A's tip fails with a merge conflict: drop the conflicting stack, bisect, or fall back to the serial path. This is the most common non-happy path in batching, and leaving it open means the implementer has to guess.

The assumption that /rebase:chain can do cross-stack assembly is unverified: Gerrit's rebase:chain rebases one change's ancestry chain onto the branch tip. Joining independent stacks into one linear chain means re-parenting stack B onto stack A's tip, i.e. rebasing onto another open change. That may need a per-change rebase with an explicit `base`, not rebase:chain. The plan presents the reuse as given without a spike. The repository does not contain S2's implementation or the gerrit-verify.yaml workflow the plan references, so neither claim can be checked against code.

The mechanism for recording the run_id is unspecified: AC2 requires dispatching gerrit-verify.yaml and recording that run's run_id, but the plan never says how the run_id is obtained. The workflow file the plan references does not exist in this repository, so it gives no basis for assuming a mechanism. The plan also does not show how a per-change concurrency group behaves when a re-batch dispatches against a new combined-tip change.

No testing plan: There are no tests or verification steps for assembly ordering, the BATCH_MAX cap, the N=5 bound and serial fallback, the single-dispatch behaviour, or the handoff record's contents. The acceptance criteria are behavioural claims with no stated evidence kind.

The BATCH_MAX=8 rationale is incoherent: The cap is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap'. But the plan triggers one run on the combined tip, so that run's job count does not depend on how many members are in the batch. The plan itself also says the concurrent-run count is not the limiter. The real trade-off is blast radius versus failure-bisection cost, which S9 has to handle.

Batch-state storage and lifecycle are undefined: S7 writes the handoff record 'to the batch state', but the plan never says where that state lives, who creates or clears it, or how it behaves across re-batches, a crash or restart, and fallback to serial. This shared state is the contract between S7, S8 and S9.

The plan says the Phase-1 single-wipChain invariant no longer holds, but its only mitigation is for main advancing. It does not define mutual exclusion between the Phase-2 batcher and the Phase-1 serial lander, nor between overlapping batches. The same change could be selected, rebased and dispatched by both paths concurrently.

AC2 says the story triggers 'exactly ONE CI run on the combined tip', but the FFO TOCTOU AC re-assembles and re-batches when main advances. A re-assembled chain has a new tip SHA and needs a fresh CI run, so one batch can incur up to 1+5 runs. The two ACs contradict each other as written.

AC2 and AC3 contradict each other. The TOCTOU re-check runs 'immediately before the batch is handed off', i.e. after CI is green. A re-assembly there produces a new tip that must be re-tested, so up to N=5 CI runs can occur, not exactly ONE. The plan does not say whether re-batch re-dispatches CI. It also does not address the window remaining between S7's handoff and S8's submit.

Nothing says what happens when a stack can't be rebased cleanly onto the growing combined chain. The What section assumes 'N non-conflicting changes', but stacks that rebase cleanly onto main can still conflict with each other once they are chained. S9 covers CI failure, not conflicts during assembly.

The cross-stack assembly algorithm is under-specified on several points. (a) Order: in what order are stacks stacked onto main (FIFO by Autosubmit vote time?). (b) Conflicts: how is 'non-conflicting' determined, and what happens to a stack whose rebase onto the growing chain conflicts? (c) Over-cap stacks: when a single stack has more than BATCH_MAX members, or adding the next stack would exceed 8, is the stack split, skipped, or allowed? (d) Re-parenting: /rebase:chain rebases an existing chain onto a base, but re-parenting stack B onto stack A's tip is a different operation (e.g. rebase with base=<A tip>).

The plan assumes members are 'non-conflicting' but defines no behavior when S2's /rebase:chain fails during cross-stack assembly. Examples: stack B does not rebase cleanly onto stack A's tip, or a member has an unmet dependency.

The plan assumes Gerrit's `/rebase:chain` endpoint can join separate stacks into one chain without checking that it can. The endpoint rebases one linear ancestry, with the operated change as the tip. Putting stack B on top of stack A's tip requires re-parenting the chain onto a specific change (RebaseInput `base`). Gerrit doc versions disagree on whether chain rebase accepts that option, and the plan pins no Gerrit version and gives no call shape. S2 probably uses rebase:chain only to rebase onto the branch tip.

AC1 relies on S2's `/rebase:chain` as 'the building block for cross-stack chain assembly'. Gerrit's rebase-chain endpoint rebases one existing ancestry chain (the operated change plus its ancestors) onto its target branch. Nothing confirms that it can put an *independent* stack B on top of stack A's tip to build one combined linear chain. That would need a per-change `base` override or a change to each stack's root parent. This is the central technical move of the story, and it is unverified.
Value validation is missing. The Why claims batching collapses ~N×CI to ~1 CI cycle, but no criterion measures it, e.g. before/after queue-to-land time for N queued changes, or the fallback rate.

The leaf introduces non-trivial new logic but has no testing criteria: assembly, cap enforcement, a bounded re-batch loop with fallback, and dispatch against real Gerrit and GHA boundaries. Nothing requires a live end-to-end exercise of dispatch→run_id→handoff record against a real combined-tip change. That leaves the path satisfiable by mocked-only coverage that never hits the Gerrit/GHA boundary.

The 'batch state' that S7 writes and S8 reads has no stated storage location, format, or lifecycle. Options include a file, Gerrit hashtag/comment, or a DB row. The plan also does not say when the state is created, superseded on re-batch, or cleared.

The BATCH_MAX=8 justification ('sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap') contradicts the Why section, which says the concurrent-run count isn't the limiter. The value is asserted rather than derived from any measured job budget or runtime.

The BATCH_MAX=8 rationale ('sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap') does not follow from the design. A single gerrit-verify run on the tip runs the same jobs regardless of member count, and the Why section says concurrency is not the limiter. The real tradeoff is not stated: larger batches cost more on failure and bisection.

The reason given for BATCH_MAX=8 ('sized to one run's job budget') doesn't hold up. A single CI run on the combined tip tests one tree, so its job count doesn't depend on how many members are in it. The real cost of a large batch is how likely it is to fail, and how expensive it is to find the culprit (S9) or re-run when main moves.

The plan does not handle failure of the single CI dispatch. Undefined cases: workflow_dispatch rejected or erroring, no run appearing, a run stuck in queued/in-progress (likely under the Free-tier cap), and how run_id is reliably correlated to the dispatch. There is no timeout and no retry/backoff.

Every re-batch caused by main advancing means a full new CI cycle, because the re-assembled tip has a new SHA. With N=5, a single batch can cost up to 6 CI cycles before falling back to serial, which undercuts the '~1 CI cycle' promise. The plan doesn't acknowledge this cost or say what triggers the re-check.

The plan's reason for BATCH_MAX=8 ('sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap') contradicts the plan's own Why section, which says the concurrent-run count is not the limiter. It also doesn't explain how member count affects the job budget of a single combined-tip run. As written, the limit looks borrowed (cargo-cult) rather than worked out.

Assembling the combined chain mutates the members. Rebasing independent stacks onto each other creates new patchsets that make unrelated changes Gerrit-dependent on one another. The plan gives no back-out step to un-chain members when a batch is dropped to the Phase-1 serial path after N=5 attempts, or when a member is removed. Red-CI handling is deferred to S9, but the N=5 drop path is owned by S7.

The FFO re-check runs 'immediately before the batch is handed off', but S8 then casts N votes and submits. main can advance between the S7 hand-off and S8's submit, so the stale-tree guarantee does not hold at submit time unless S8 re-checks. The plan does not say who owns that final check.

Rejecting every body that starts with '-' breaks ordinary markdown bullet comments: AC1 rejects any body argument that begins with `-`. Agents routinely write comments that open with a markdown list item ("- fixed X\n- verified Y") or a checklist ("- [ ] ..."). Under this rule, every existing caller that writes such bodies would start failing. The plan treats this breaking change as acceptable without saying so or justifying it, and it pushes the burden onto the `--` escape hatch, which current callers do not use. A narrower check would catch the reported failures without the breakage: reject only tokens that look like an option, such as `^--?[A-Za-z][\w-]*$` with no whitespace, or an exact match for known-misused flags.
